 Gold prices have fallen nearly 8% in a month. What will drive the next move?
 Gold prices could remain supported if real yields fall, central banks continue buying, the dollar weakens, ETF inflows remain strong and geopolitical uncertainty persists 
 Navneet Dubey 
 November 18, 2026 / 09:07 IST 
 Story continues below Advertisement 
 Remove Ad 
 The wedding season could support physical gold demand in India in the coming months 
 Gold prices fell nearly 8 percent from a month ago.
 US rates, central-bank buying, and dollar drive outlook.
 Experts advise staggered investments and portfolio balance.
 Did our AI summary help?

 Gold prices have come under pressure after a strong rally, with 10 grams of 24-carat gold in Ahmedabad falling to Rs 1.39 lakh on November 17 from around Rs 1.5 lakh a month ago, a decline of nearly 8 percent. While India's wedding season is beginning and could support jewellery demand, the outlook for gold will increasingly depend on global factors such as US interest rates, dollar movements, central-bank purchases and investor demand. 
 Here are six factors that could determine where gold prices head next. 
 US interest rates and Fed policy 
 Gold does not pay interest, making it more attractive when returns on other investments fall. Markets will closely track US inflation, jobs data and signals from the Federal Reserve (Fed) to understand the direction of interest rates. 
 “Real yields matter more than headline rates. If nominal rates stay flat while inflation expectations fall, real yields rise, which is a headwind for gold. If inflation cools and the Fed turns more accommodative, the case for gold strengthens. Persistently high inflation with rates held higher for longer could mean volatile, range-bound prices,” said Amit Modak, Director, PNGS. 
 Central-bank buying 
 Central banks have emerged as a major source of gold demand. They bought 321 tonnes in Q3, taking purchases in 2026 to 675 tonnes, up 6 percent year-on-year. The World Gold Council (WGC) expects full-year purchases to at least match 2025 levels. 
 Countries are adding gold to their reserves to reduce dependence on the US dollar and protect against geopolitical and financial risks. This buying can support prices even when jewellery demand weakens. However, central banks may slow purchases when prices rise sharply and buy more when prices fall. 
 “Central banks have become gold's most dependable buyer. What stands out to us is that they kept accumulating even with prices near record highs, while retail buyers stepped back. That isn't a trade. It's a strategic rethink of how reserves are built. As long as countries want reserves that no single government can freeze or print, gold has a buyer of last resort,” said Vedant Gupte, Co-Founder and CEO of investment platform Trackk. 
 Dollar and rupee movements 
 Gold prices generally rise when the US dollar weakens and come under pressure when it strengthens. For Indian buyers, the rupee is equally important. A weaker rupee can make imported gold more expensive even if international prices remain unchanged. A stronger rupee can soften the impact of a global price increase. 
 Import duty, GST and local premiums also influence the final price buyers pay. 
 Gold ETFs and investment demand 
 High prices may discourage jewellery purchases, but investment demand through gold exchange-traded funds (ETFs), bars and coins can support the market. More investors, including younger buyers, are also looking at gold as an investment rather than just an ornament. 
 ETF flows offer an indication of investor sentiment. 
 “Global gold ETFs added 211t in Q3, reversing Q2 outflows. The inflows came despite higher bond yields and a stronger dollar, which signals conviction. Continued inflows can sustain prices, while a reversal may signal profit-taking. Bar and coin demand is the other indicator to watch,” said Modak. 
 Geopolitical and economic risks 
 Wars, trade tensions, rising government debt and concerns about currencies can push investors towards gold as a safe-haven asset. However, the impact depends on how serious and prolonged these risks are. Prices may rise sharply during a crisis but can also retreat once immediate concerns ease. 
 “Trade tensions, rising public debt and geopolitical shocks can drive safe-haven buying. Their impact depends on the severity and duration of the event and on market reaction, and gold often spikes and then fades. Effects on policies post US midterm elections as a factor to watch. Concerns about debt and currency debasement can support gold as a long-term diversifier,” said Modak. 
 Jewellery demand versus investment buying 
 The wedding season could support physical gold demand in India in the coming months. Globally, however, high prices are weighing on jewellery purchases, with double-digit declines in Q3. 
 The WGC expects investment demand to remain the main driver of gold demand, with central-bank purchases providing additional support. This means weaker jewellery buying does not necessarily translate into lower gold prices if investors and central banks continue to buy. 
 Outlook: What should investors watch? 
 Gold prices could remain supported if real yields fall, central banks continue buying, the dollar weakens, ETF inflows remain strong and geopolitical uncertainty persists. However, rising yields, a stronger dollar or profit-booking by investors could trigger further corrections. 
 Key indicators to watch: 
 US inflation data and Fed commentary, the 10-year US real yield, the 
 USD/INR exchange rate, gold ETF flows, central-bank purchases and changes in India's import duty. 
 Also read: When does borrowing to invest become too risky? 3 warning signs investors should watch 
 What should investors do? 
 Gold should be treated as a portfolio diversifier rather than a short-term trading opportunity. Staggered investments can help investors avoid committing a large amount at one price. 
 “A disciplined allocation sized to your goals and risk tolerance, with staggered entry (for example SIP-style buying via ETFs, etc), works better than chasing price moves,” said Modak. 
 “For retail investors, the smarter approach is to accumulate gold rather than chase it. Staggered buying, kept to a sensible slice of the portfolio, lets you ride the structural story without being whipsawed by every Fed headline,” added Gupte.
